title: The fourth
devanagari: नान्तःप्रज्ञं न बहिःप्रज्ञं नोभयतःप्रज्ञं न प्रज्ञानघनं न प्रज्ञं नाप्रज्ञम् ।
एकात्मप्रत्ययसारं प्रपञ्चोपशमं शान्तं शिवमद्वैतं चतुर्थं मन्यन्ते । स आत्मा स विज्ञेयः ॥ ७ ॥
iast: sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt
nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiḥprajñaṃ nobhayataḥprajñaṃ na prajñānaghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam
adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam
ekātmapratyayasāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitaṃ caturthaṃ manyante | sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ
english: “For truly, everything here is Brahma; this self is Brahma. This same self has four fourths.”

“Not inwardly cognitive, not outwardly cognitive, not both-wise cognitive, not a cognition-mass, not cognitive, not non-cognitive, unseen, with which there can be no dealing, ungraspable, having no distinctive mark, non-thinkable, that cannot be designated, the essence of the assurance of which is the state of being one with the Self, the cessation of development, tranquil, benign, without a second—[such] they think is the fourth. He is the Self. He should be discerned.”
translator: Robert Ernest Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads (Oxford University Press, 1921); his Sanskrit glosses left out
edition: Sanskrit: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Sansknet project input, as on GRETIL
notes: Verses 3 to 5 name the first three fourths: the self waking, dreaming, and in deep sleep, where there is no desire and no dream. The fourth is not a fourth state that comes after them. It is what is there through all three, so the verse can only say what it is not. [P3] [C1]

Stepping out of the body to watch the day lived (V) is a picture of the witness, the second bird on the tree that eats nothing and watches. A picture is not the knowing; the verses are the teaching. [P6]
